items.title: [gwec.net] Ember analysis says adding wind cuts reliable power costs 18%
items.content_html: Adding wind to solar and batteries cuts the modeled median cost of meeting 90% of electricity demand from $105 to $86 per megawatt-hour, according to an analysis by energy think tank Ember published with the Global Wind Energy Council (GWEC). The combination reduces storage needs because wind and solar output vary at different times and across seasons. Ember estimated that three-quarters of global electricity demand could be met at the 90% threshold for under $100/MWh with wind, compared with half using solar and batteries alone. The analysis also examines the economics of planned fossil-fuel capacity: of 845 gigawatts of coal and gas plants in planning, 706 GW are in regions where firm renewable electricity with backup could cost less than $100/MWh. Ember said it modeled hourly weather from 2015 through 2024 against constant demand and described the results as a stress test, not a forecast.

items.title: [france24.com] COP31 draft calls for immediate fossil-fuel shift as nations remain divided
items.content_html: A first draft of the COP31 climate summit’s political agreement in Antalya calls for an immediate shift away from fossil fuels and increased adaptation funding. Reports describe deadly glacier flooding in Nepal and wildfires in Europe. Australia released the text on Nov. 16 for negotiations among nearly 200 countries; it includes competing proposals to “transition away” from fossil fuels or phase them out, but either could be removed before an agreement is reached. The draft also proposes at least $120 billion a year for adaptation in developing countries by 2035. Climate campaigners say it lacks a clear process for advancing fossil-fuel roadmaps and that the proposed funding would cover less than a third of estimated needs. The proposed electricity target has also drawn criticism because the text does not require the added power to come from renewable sources. Negotiators must reach consensus before the summit’s scheduled close on Nov. 20. Australia’s climate change and energy minister and lead negotiator, Chris Bowen, expects further revisions as ministers negotiate the disputed language.

items.title: [utilitydive.com] US orders Michigan coal plant to stay open despite court ruling
items.content_html:
🔧 ✏️

The U.S. Energy Department issued a seventh emergency order requiring the 64-year-old J.H. Campbell coal plant near Grand Rapids, Michigan, to keep operating for another 90 days, through mid-February 2027, despite a federal appeals court ruling in September that an earlier order was unlawful. Energy Secretary Chris Wright said the plant is needed to prevent blackouts and maintain reliable electricity supplies; the department cited lessons from Winter Storm Fern and other events during the 2026 Arctic cold period. The plant had been scheduled to retire in May 2025. Michigan and other states, along with environmental groups, challenged the earlier orders, arguing there was no qualifying emergency. The appeals court agreed, and the Energy Department has asked the full court to rehear the case. That request remains pending as the new order takes effect.

items.title: [phys.org] COP31 nations split over 1.5°C goal as threshold nears
items.content_html: Halfway through the COP31 climate negotiations in Antalya, countries are divided over whether to keep the 1.5°C warming limit as a central goal after the United Nations said in September that crossing it was imminent and unavoidable. Global temperatures have risen about 1.4°C above pre-industrial levels. Some countries want the summit’s final decision to reaffirm 1.5°C as the “right goal” and call for temperatures to return below that limit as soon as possible. Other negotiators, including members of the Arab Group and Like-Minded Developing Countries, are pushing to weaken or remove references to the target. Scientists say reversing an overshoot would require sharp emissions cuts and large-scale carbon removal over decades; University of Exeter climate scientist Pierre Friedlingstein described that prospect as “extremely ambitious”.

items.title: [winnipegfreepress.com] Federal memo warns freshwater pressures threaten Canada’s long-term security
items.content_html: An internal federal memo warns that growing pressure on freshwater supplies could harm Canada’s long-term security and prosperity. It says it is unclear whether the country can meet future needs as its cities and economy grow. The Canada Water Agency prepared the document for Environment Minister Julie Dabrusin as work proceeds on a national water security strategy. Dabrusin called the strategy a “mission critical priority” in response to Prime Minister Mark Carney’s request for cabinet priorities. The memo links water risks to climate change, pollution, population growth, overuse and aging infrastructure. Public consultation ran from Sept. 9 to Oct. 25, and the agency also consulted provincial, territorial and Indigenous partners. The memo calls for an assessment of water protection and sustainable management, including shared waters with the United States and global water risks. The 12-page memo was obtained through an access-to-information request, with some material withheld.

Police estimated attendance at more than 7,000; organizers put the crowd at 10,000. The United Nations COP31 climate conference, which opened Nov. 9 and runs through Nov. 20, had reached its midpoint, with nearly 200 countries working toward an agreement. Negotiators remain divided over adaptation finance, climate science and the shift from fossil fuels to clean energy. Proposals for the conference’s overarching agreement had yet to be turned into a draft, expected early the following week. The adaptation-finance text included competing options. Ministers were arriving to tackle the hardest issues before the conference closes on Nov. 20.

items.title: [theguardian.com] Climate-driven extreme weather kills tens of thousands worldwide in 2026
items.content_html: Fires, heat waves, floods and storms have killed tens of thousands of people across multiple continents in 2026, a toll described as a conservative estimate. The year followed the hottest summer since records began in 1850, according to the Guardian’s review of events through July. In February, record rainfall triggered landslides in Brazil that killed 72 people and displaced more than 10,000; floods in Ethiopia killed at least 131 in March, and heat-related deaths were reported across South Asia in May. The World Meteorological Organization said the oceans store more than 90% of the excess energy in Earth’s system, while atmospheric carbon dioxide continued to rise.

items.title: [indiatoday.in] India rejects Turkey's voluntary 2035 electrification pledge at COP31
items.content_html: Turkey is urging countries at the U.N. climate summit COP31 in Antalya to raise electricity’s share of global final energy use from about 23% to 35% by 2035, but India says it will not sign the voluntary pledge. New Delhi argues that negotiations should prioritize financing for clean-energy infrastructure rather than add another target. It also wants developed countries’ climate support to come from public sources on affordable terms, rather than through loans that add to debt. India also objects that the pledge counts electricity regardless of how it is generated, so coal-fired power would qualify. The European Commission has backed the initiative. COP31 began on November 9, and Environment Minister Bhupender Yadav is due to join ministerial sessions in the summit’s second week.

items.title: [insideclimatenews.org] Georgia Power assigns batteries 20% capacity rating in 2032-33 procurement
items.content_html: Georgia Power, Georgia’s largest electric utility, is preparing to procure 2,000 to 6,000 megawatts of capacity for 2032 and 2033 as data-center growth and electrification increase expected demand. For this procurement, it assigns battery storage an effective load carrying capability (ELCC)—the share of a resource’s capacity counted as reliably available—of 20%. That means a 1,000-megawatt battery project counts as 200 megawatts, compared with 800 megawatts for a gas plant rated at 80% ELCC. Clean-energy advocates say the lower rating could disadvantage batteries and favor gas. Georgia Power says its evaluations are consistent and accurate but has not disclosed details of its calculation. The utility is reviewing proposals and expects to discuss projects with regulators early in 2027, with selected projects due for regulatory approval in mid-2027.

items.title: [scmp.com] China targets 300 million kilowatts of energy storage by 2030
items.content_html: China plans to raise installed new energy storage capacity to 300 million kilowatts by 2030 under a joint plan from the National Development and Reform Commission and National Energy Administration. The plan also sets a target average storage duration of about three hours and aims to shift the sector from rapid expansion to market-driven growth. Separately, China expects new clean-energy generation to meet all growth in power demand by 2030, China Central Television reported, citing an Academy of Macroeconomic Research report. Renewable generation topped 3 trillion kilowatt-hours in the first nine months of 2026 and accounted for more than 40% of total output, CCTV said. China is also seeking to revise its Renewable Energy Law, with draft provisions covering grid coordination, green hydrogen and equipment recycling. The public-comment period closes Dec. 5. In the nuclear sector, the Ningde plant is using digital inspection systems while building two additional reactors.

items.title: [rfi.fr] COP31 climate science dispute threatens 2028 emissions progress review
items.content_html: Negotiators at COP31 in Antalya are divided over whether the U.N. climate science panel’s next assessments will be ready for the 2028 global review of emissions progress. The European Union and dozens of countries want publication before then, while Saudi Arabia, India and China support delaying the reports until 2029. The dispute concerns the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change’s (IPCC) seventh assessment, which will examine climate change and options for adaptation and emissions cuts. Governments use the panel’s findings to assess collective progress under the Paris Agreement. A climate scientist who contributed to earlier assessments said decisions should use current rather than seven-year-old evidence. The IPCC’s October meeting ended without agreement, and the timing dispute is now part of the wider COP31 negotiations. A separate report by the Kick Big Polluters Out coalition counted 103 companies and industry groups at the summit, including 60 from the fossil-fuel sector. It said their delegations outnumbered those of several climate-vulnerable countries. Climate TRACE estimates that electrification powered by clean energy could cut global emissions by 14%, compared with 7% if fossil fuels are also used.

items.title: [phys.org] IOM chief warns climate risks could displace over 200 million
items.content_html: Amy Pope, director general of the International Organization for Migration (IOM), warned at the United Nations climate conference, COP31, in Antalya, Turkey, that more than 200 million people living in highly climate-vulnerable communities are at risk of displacement. IOM data show storms, drought, wildfires, extreme temperatures and floods forced nearly 30 million people from their homes in 2025. Pope said governments spend billions of dollars on border security while underfunding adaptation measures that could help communities remain in place. She estimated the cost of those measures at about $310 billion, compared with roughly $30 billion in funding so far. She argued that helping communities adapt before displacement occurs is more humane and cost-effective than responding to irregular migration after it begins.

items.title: [powermag.com] Battery storage firms announce $116 million supply pact and $145 million financing
items.content_html: From Nov. 10 to 13, U.S. energy storage companies announced a $116 million battery supply agreement, a $145 million debt facility and a preferred-equity investment in residential solar-and-battery projects. Battery supplier NeoVolta Power will deliver U.S.-manufactured, foreign-entity-of-concern-compliant systems in 2027; Calibrant Energy’s financing will fund solar and storage projects, including a system for a large data center customer. Energy investment firm Captona’s project-level investment covers 9,400 Sunrun residential projects across more than 20 states, totaling 74 megawatts of solar and 110 megawatt-hours of batteries. Calibrant did not disclose how it would allocate the financing among projects or the data center system’s location and power capacity.

items.title: [independent.co.uk] Super El Niño warms Pacific, threatens California marine life and snowpack
items.content_html: The U.S. National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration’s (NOAA) Climate Prediction Center said the developing El Niño is likely to remain strong to very strong through March 2027, with ocean temperatures still rising. The event is already associated with unusually warm waters off California, higher coastal water levels and changes in marine food supplies. Scientists report seabirds washing ashore and kelp forests under stress. The pattern can shift rainfall and temperature, and forecasters expect warmer winters in the Northwest that could reduce snowpack by raising snow levels. Scientists also warn that warm Pacific waters can increase the risk of coastal flooding when high tides coincide with storms. NOAA’s outlook says the event is expected to weaken early next year, while reports indicate its effects could continue into spring.

items.title: [gwec.net] Wind industry seeks faster permits and doubled investment to expand capacity
items.content_html: The Global Wind Energy Council (GWEC), an industry group, and the Turkish Wind Energy Association launched a declaration at the COP31 climate summit in Antalya on Nov. 13, calling for faster wind development and outlining how global capacity could reach 4 terawatts by 2035. GWEC projects capacity will reach 2 terawatts by 2029 and 3 terawatts by 2035; reaching 4 terawatts would require stronger government support to reduce project risks and attract investment. The plan calls for predictable policies, faster permitting, upgraded grids, better access to finance and stronger supply chains. GWEC chief executive Ben Backwell said offshore wind farms can take two years to build but eight to 12 years to secure permits. Wind industry leaders also said doubling investment could lift annual capacity additions above 300 gigawatts.

items.title: [energynow.com] Norway’s Supreme Court invalidates three oilfield permits over emissions reviews
items.content_html: Norway’s Supreme Court on Nov. 13 invalidated government approvals for the North Sea oilfields Breidablikk, Tyrving and Yggdrasil, ruling that environmental reviews should have assessed emissions from burning the extracted oil, not just from production. The six-to-five decision requires the Energy Ministry to reconsider the permits under proper procedures but does not order operators to stop work. Equinor’s Breidablikk and Aker BP’s Tyrving are producing, and Yggdrasil is scheduled to start production in 2027. Environmental groups Greenpeace Norway and Young Friends of the Earth brought the case against the state in 2023. The court said the oil companies were not parties to the case, so the ruling does not automatically suspend their operations. The campaigners’ lawyer said they would consider bringing a separate case against the operators. The ministry said it would re-examine the permits. The government has said it has changed its practice to include emissions from burning oil and gas in assessments for new fields.
